Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "The watering rota at North Glasshouse covers the propagation benches, the two tomato bays, and the narrow house of herbs. It is pinned beside the sink, where the crew can check it while filling cans, and a smaller copy hangs on the door of the tool shed. The rota runs from Monday through Sunday, with the early round beginning at 7:30 and the late round at 3:00. Each entry names the person responsible and the zone to be checked. It is a working schedule rather than a record of every plant watered, so anyone who changes a round writes the adjustment on both copies.

Mara coordinates the week and checks the moisture trays on Monday morning. She waters the propagation benches herself on that round because the young seedlings dry faster than the established plants. Dev takes the tomato bays on Monday afternoon and Thursday morning. He checks the soil at the base of each row before watering, since the outer beds hold moisture longer than the beds beside the ventilation fans. On the rota, those two areas are marked “outer rows” and “fan rows” to avoid treating the whole bay as if it needed the same amount.

The herb house is assigned to Joel on Tuesday and Friday, but the arrangement is not a standing instruction to water every pot. He checks the rosemary, sage, and thyme first, then compares the smaller pots with the moisture notes on their labels. Mint and parsley are kept on the lower bench, where the shade cloth makes the surface stay damp well into the afternoon. Joel leaves those pots alone if the compost is still moist below the surface. If he does water them, he records the time beside the date so the next person can distinguish a fresh round from an earlier check.

1. Before starting a round, the assigned person checks the rain gauge outside the east door and reads the moisture note left by the previous shift. The greenhouse roof is sound, but wind sometimes carries rain through the open louvres, especially near the herb house. A wet path does not by itself mean that the beds have received enough water. The note should identify the affected zone, not simply say “rain.” If the gauge is empty and the ground outside is dry, the usual checks still apply.

On Wednesday, Lin covers the propagation benches while Mara attends the seed inventory. Lin follows the labels on the trays, including the ones marked for reduced watering after pricking out. The trays on the middle bench are not all at the same stage, although they share a shelf, and Lin checks their individual notes rather than relying on the bench label alone. A blue tag means that a tray was misted, not that it was watered through. The tag is removed only after the next scheduled check, so it may still be present when the compost has begun to dry.

The rota has a space at the bottom for cover arrangements. If someone cannot make a round, they contact the next person listed for that zone and write the change on the sheet. Mara said, “Please leave a note if you swap a round; I can’t tell from an empty box whether it was covered or missed.” No one is expected to take over an entire day without checking the other person’s schedule first. The Sunday round is shared: Dev checks the tomato bays before lunch, and Joel checks the herb house later in the afternoon. Mara takes the propagation area only if the trays need attention.

The water supply is controlled by the two taps beside the mixing bench. The left tap feeds the hose reel for the tomato bays, while the right tap fills cans for the propagation benches and herb house. Neither tap should be left running while someone moves between zones. The hose nozzle is kept on its narrow setting for the tomato beds, but cans are used around seedlings and pots because the hose can disturb their compost. After use, the hose is wound onto the reel without a tight kink at the connector; a kink has made the flow uneven before, even though the tap itself was open.

When a plant looks wilted despite damp compost, the assigned person checks the leaves and stem before adding more water. The ventilation fans can make the tomato leaves droop temporarily on warm afternoons, and watering in response to that alone can leave the lower soil saturated. Any persistent change is noted on the board beside the plant label, with the bay and row included. The rota does not replace those notes: it tells the crew who is checking each area, while the board keeps the detail needed for the next inspection.

At the end of each week, the old sheet goes into the blue folder in the office, and Mara pins up the next rota before the Monday round. She carries forward recurring appointments and any zone-specific notes that still apply, but she does not copy temporary observations as if they were permanent instructions. The folder also contains the greenhouse map, a current list of staff contact numbers, and spare blank sheets.
